segments.text: The arguments surrounding artificial intelligence are getting louder.
The reason for this intensity is simple.
The technology is advancing at blazing speeds.
To understand any debate about the future of AI,
you have to look at the baseline of what AI can actually do,
and recognize how rapidly that baseline is moving beneath our feet.
Look at this comparison mapping AI capabilities.
This shows how drastically the technology evolves in just three years.
First, look at answering.
In 2023, the instant you had entered,
the model started typing with whatever came out first.
By 2026, a model can work quietly on a hard problem for several minutes
before it says a single word.
Next is image generation.
Ask a 2023 model for a picture of a dog,
and it might return a flawed image with a bonus leg or rabbit ears.
In 2026, the output includes photorealistic images
with legible background signs and full video complete with sound and dialogue.
Then there is the context window.
The free chatbots most people used in 2023
could only hold a few pages in memory at once.
Current models can hold a million tokens.
That places an entire series of novels and view at the exact same time.
Finally, look at taking action.
In 2023, AI gave you a list of steps to accomplish a task.
By 2026, AI agents can actively book flights,
build software, and fix code errors right in front of you.
The definition of what an AI is capable of
shifts completely in a very short window of time.
This rapid release cycle is driven by market forces.
AI companies are in a fierce race to dominate the industry,
pushing them to release new models every couple of months.
A limitation can disappear quickly,
so today's no is not necessarily permanent.
This diagram outlines what exactly is driving this relentless acceleration.
There are three mechanical concepts pushing the technology forward.
The first driver is better training.
AI models learn from data.
As companies feed them more and better data,
the models become more accurate and produce better results.
The second driver is more compute.
Running these models require massive amounts of chips housed in data centers,
and the major companies are spending billions of dollars right now
to increase that computing power.
The third driver is that AI helps build AI.
On well-defined tasks,
the strongest models can write code for the next generation of models
much faster than human programmers.
Slow down and consider that third concept again.
AI is already helping people build better AI.
Look at this conceptual map of the future.
The first is automated AI research.
Currently, AI can write code, run experiments, and analyze results.
But human researchers still set the goals and verify the work.
The second idea is self-improving AI.
This is an unproven state where an AI improves its own design
to create a stronger version and then repeats the process
with little to no human direction.
Note the distinction.
One is human-directed.
The other would be a self-reinforcing loop.
Using an AI tool to help write code is a reality today.
An AI upgrading its own underlying architecture on its own
is entirely hypothetical.
That brings us to the ultimate question of how far AI can actually go.
This spectrum highlights the two most debated concepts.
The first is AGI, or artificial general intelligence.
This refers to human level ability across many kinds of work.
However, there is no agreed finish line.
Further out is ASI, or artificial superintelligence.
This is a purely hypothetical state where AI exceeds the best humans
across nearly every cognitive field.
Nobody knows if building this is even possible.
Nobody knows whether AI will reach either milestone.
These are theoretical concepts to help you navigate the discussion,
not a guaranteed timeline of future events.
AI keeps getting faster and more powerful.
Nobody is sure where it stops.
